topics.description: The 1940 German campaign that defeated France by advancing through the Ardennes and led to the establishment of the Vichy regime.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: The launch of this military campaign ended an eight-month period of relative inaction dubbed  the “Phony War.” Maxime Weygand's (max-EEM VAY-gah's) planned counterattack failed to stop  this campaign. The Second Armistice at Compiègne (kahm-PEN-yeh) was signed just six weeks  after the start of this campaign, which took a route through the (*) Ardennes (ARD-en) Forest that  bypassed the Maginot (MAA-jin-oh) Line and led to the creation of the Vichy (VEE-shee) government.  For 10 points, name this World War II Nazi-led campaign whose outcome forced Charles de Gaulle  (SHARL day GOAL) to flee to Britain.
parts.answer: Battle of France [or German invasion of France; or Axis defeat of France in World War  II; or Nazi invasion of France until “Nazi” is read]

topics.description: A mass protest movement in Hong Kong sparked by a proposed extradition bill and expanded into demands for democratic reform and government accountability.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: An event in this city led to the blinding of Indonesian journalist Veby Mega Indah, and was partially inspired by lack of political change following the Umbrella Revolution. Protesters in this city sought the resignation of Carrie Lam. Protests in this city were sparked by a bill that would have allowed (*) extradition to Taiwan and mainland China. For ten points, name this special administrative region of China.
parts.answer: Hong Kong [accept HKSAR or Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People’s Republic of China; prompt on People’s Republic of China or Zhongguo or Zhōnghuá Rénmín Gònghéguó]

topics.description: Missionary settlements in South America, especially Paraguay, that combined Catholic evangelization with self-sustaining agricultural and livestock enterprises.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Antonio Ruiz de Montoya wrote the first grammar of the Guaraní (gwah-rah-NEE) language while working at one of these facilities. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name these large, priest-run farms, mostly found in Paraguay, which were both missionary bases and economically self-sustaining plantations for cattle or yerba mate (YAIR-bah MAH-tay).
parts.answer: reductions [or reducción; or reducciones; or redução; or reduçoes; accept, but do not otherwise reveal, Jesuit reductions]

parts.label: B
parts.question: This Catholic order, which includes Pope Francis, was founded by Ignatius of Loyola and operated the Paraguayan reductions.
parts.answer: Jesuits [or Society of Jesus]

parts.label: C
parts.question: In this country, local Guaraní called Chiriguanos (sheer-ee-GWAH-nos) resisted evangelization prior to the 1892 Battle of Kuruyuki (koo-roo-YOO-kee). The coca-raising Aymara (AI-MAR-ah) people live mostly in this country.
parts.answer: Bolivia [Plurinational State of Bolivia; or Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia; or Tetã Hetãvoregua Mborivia; or Wuliwya Walja Suyunakana Marka; or Puliwya Achka Aylluska Mamallaqta]

topics.description: A southeastern African country where the FRELIMO government fought the RENAMO insurgency during a Cold War-era civil war.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about Cuban involvement in African wars, for 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Cuban soldiers were sent in to fight for one of these two countries over their disputed region of Ogaden. These two countries were led by Siad Barre and Mengistu during the Ogaden War between them.
parts.answer: Somalia AND Ethiopia [accept answers in either order; accept Federal Republic of Somalia or Soomaaliya or Jamhuuriyadda Federaalkaa Soomaaliya for Somalia; accept Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia or Ityop’iya Federalawi Demokrasiyawi Ripeblik for Ethiopia; reject partial answers]

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] Along with the Soviet Union, Cuba supported Samora Machel and his FRELIMO party in this country’s civil war. This country’s opposition party RENAMO wanted the AK-47 to be removed from its flag.
parts.answer: Mozambique [or Republic of Mozambique or Republica de Moçambique]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] Troops from this longtime Communist leader’s Cuba helped the MPLA in Angola’s Battle of Cuito Cuanavale.
parts.answer: Fidel Castro [or Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz; prompt on Castro alone]

topics.description: A 371 BCE battle in which Theban forces under Epaminondas decisively defeated Sparta and weakened its dominance in Greece.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: A king of this city died after losing to Epaminondas at the Battle of Leuctra (LEWK-truh). The agoge (AH-goh-gay) system of this city trained children for the military and was invented by Lycurgus. Another king of this city was defeated in battle after a shepherd led the Persian army around the pass at (*) Thermopylae. For ten points, what rival of Athens was home to the famous 300 and was known for its warrior culture?
parts.answer: Sparta

topics.description: A powerful Florentine banking and ruling dynasty that sponsored artists and shaped the politics and culture of Renaissance and early modern Italy.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Answer the following about the Italian Baroque [bah-ROHK] artist Artemisia Gentileschi [ahr-teh-MEE-see-ah JEN-tih-LES-kee], for ten points each.

parts.label: A
parts.question: After being assaulted in her father’s studio, Artemisia frequently painted biblical scenes in which women, like Judith and Jael, do this to their enemies, Holofernes and Sisera.
parts.answer: killing them (accept synonyms like murder; accept descriptions like “driving a nail through the temple or beheading)

parts.label: B
parts.question: Like many of her contemporaries, Artemisia worked for years in this Italian city. Her painting Judith Slaying Holofernes is displayed in this city’s Uffizi Gallery [oo-FEET-zee Gallery].
parts.answer: Florence (accept Firenze)

parts.label: C
parts.question: While in Florence, Artemisia was patronized by members of this powerful banking family founded by Cosimo.
parts.answer: Medici (accept House of Medici)

topics.description: Protective headgear used by soldiers during World War I, including the Adrian, Brodie, Pickelhaube, and Stahlhelm designs.
aliases: Combat helmets of World War I

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: One of these objects designed in 1915 by Louis Adrian [loo-ee ay-dree-un] had a distinct ridge at the top and was adopted by the French Army. Another of them designed by John Leopold Brodie was nicknamed the “doughboy” by American soldiers. Frederick William IV designed one of these objects made of boiled leather, called the Pickelhaube [pickle-how-buh], which had a (*) distinctive upward spike. In 1916 Germany introduced a steel type of these objects whose “coal scuttle” shape was widely used in propaganda. This worn piece of equipment protected soldiers from falling shrapnel during World War I. For 10 points, name this piece of armor worn on the head.
parts.answer: World War I helmets [accept Adrian helmets or Brodie helmets or Stahlhelme]

topics.description: A late-17th-century Scottish colonial project that attempted to establish a settlement at Darién in Panama and contributed to Scotland’s financial crisis before the 1707 Act of Union.

parts.label: L
parts.question: The failure of this plan wreaked havoc on the Scottish economy because about 20 percent of all the money circulating in Scotland was dedicated to backing it. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: [H] Name this scheme that sought to establish a Scottish settlement in modern-day Panama. The failure of this scheme and the resulting bankruptcy of the Scottish government led them to accept the Act of Union with England.
parts.answer: Darien scheme

parts.label: B
parts.question: [M] This dynasty’s final ruler, Queen Anne, became the monarch of a united Great Britain with the Act of Union in 1707. James I was the first king of England from this dynasty that followed the Tudors.
parts.answer: Stuarts [accept House of Stuart]

parts.label: C
parts.question: [E] The Act of Union gave rise to the Scottish branch of this 18th-century intellectual movement which emphasized rational thought. Adam Smith and David Hume were part of the Scottish branch of this movement.
parts.answer: the Enlightenment [or the Age of Enlightenment or the Age of Reason; accept the Scottish Enlightenment]

topics.description: The last Bourbon king of France, Charles X reigned from 1824 until his overthrow in the July Revolution of 1830.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This king's prime minister, Jules de Polignac (zhool day pah-lin-YAK), issued the Four Ordinances at  Saint-Cloud. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this last Bourbon king of France, who succeeded Louis XVIII (the eighteenth) in 1824 and  was toppled by the July Revolution in 1830.
parts.answer: Charles X (the tenth) [or Charles Philippe, Count of Artois; prompt on Charles]

parts.label: B
parts.question: This “Citizen King” elevated longtime ally François Guizot (FRAN-swah gee-ZOH) to prime  minister in 1847. This only Orléanist (UR-lee-AHN-ist) king of France took power when Charles X  stepped down and himself abdicated in 1848 after the June Days.
parts.answer: Louis Philippe I (the first)

parts.label: C
parts.question: Louis Philippe won out in 1830 over supporters of restoring the house of this French emperor, who  was defeated at the Battle of Waterloo.
parts.answer: Napoleon I (the first) [or Napoleon Bonaparte]

topics.description: A series of eighth- and ninth-century Byzantine disputes and imperial policies over whether the veneration of religious images constituted idolatry.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Jonah 2:8 claims that those who engage in this practice “forsake the hope of steadfast love.” John of Damascus’ arguments that a certain practice was not an example of this practice were accepted at the Second Council of Nicaea (“nigh-SEE-uh”). In Islam, the only sin that will not be forgiven without repentance is this practice, which is called shirk. In the 8th century, Byzantine Emperor (*) Leo III banned a dif erent practice on the grounds that it was an example of this practice. Moses breaks the two Tablets of the Law when he sees his people performing this practice with a golden calf. For 10 points, the First Commandment forbids what practice in which people worship things that are not God?
parts.answer: idolatry [or any answers involving idols; accept polytheism; prompt on descriptions such as praying to statues or worshiping things other than God; do NOT accept or prompt on “venerating icons” or other answers involving icons] (The Second Council of Nicaea resolved the iconoclast controversy.)
